title: Automating Antenna Pattern Testing
text:
Context
Our clinic team is helping The Aerospace Corporation and the FAA evaluate a Controlled Reception Pattern Antenna (CRPA), a GPS anti-jamming antenna, to inform whether CRPAs can be used for commercial aviation safety. The end goal is element-level and array-level characterization of the CRPA inside an anechoic chamber.
Before testing the CRPA, we are validating our measurement process on a simpler Fixed Reception Pattern Antenna (FRPA), a NovAtel GPS antenna. Measuring a radiation pattern means pointing the antenna at many known angles and recording its response with a Vector Network Analyzer (VNA) at each one. That requires two things:

a way to hold the antenna securely in the chamber, and
a way to set its angle accurately and repeatably.

title: Automating Antenna Pattern Testing
text:
My Role
I’m leading the automation of the AntRunner positioner, the motorized mount that rotates the antenna through each angle. I’m also on the mechanical team. My responsibilities:

Software: writing the Python control script that drives the positioner’s rotors, run from a Raspberry Pi that sends commands to the AntRunner’s ESP32 controller.
Mechanical team: supporting the design, assembly, and implementation of the antenna mount and positioner in the chamber.
Electrical setup: wiring and powering the AntRunner and antenna inside the chamber.
Manual baseline: I built the wooden mount used for our first, hand-rotated FRPA radiation-pattern test.
Fixturing and RF testing: machining mounting fixtures for the positioning turntables and running benchtop VNA measurements with dual probe antennas.

title: Automating Antenna Pattern Testing
text:
What I Built
We’ve measured the FRPA’s radiation pattern two ways, so we can compare a manual setup against an automated one.





Manual setup. The wooden mount I built holds the FRPA on a turntable with a printed degree scale. We rotated it by hand and read the VNA at each angle.







Automated setup. The FRPA mounted on the AntRunner positioner, which has a stepper motor for azimuth in the base and a second rotation axis in the head for elevation.

title: Automating Antenna Pattern Testing
text:
How It Works
The Python script runs a raster sweep: it steps across azimuth at a fixed elevation, then raises the elevation and sweeps again.

  
    
  

Automated FRPA test in the anechoic chamber: 10° azimuth steps every 3 seconds from −90° to +90°, then a 10° elevation step.


Build a manual baseline. I built a wooden mount and ran a hand-rotated pattern measurement with the VNA (Nov 4).
Mount the AntRunner in the chamber. The positioner slides into an adapter tube on the chamber mast and is clamped with thumbscrews. The FRPA bolts to the elevation bracket.
Write the control script. Python on a Raspberry Pi sends move commands to the AntRunner’s ESP32, which drives the rotors.
Run the raster sweep. The script steps azimuth by 10° every 3 seconds from −90° to +90°. It then raises elevation by 10°, returns to −90° azimuth, and repeats.
Compare the automated and manual patterns (Nov 11) to see whether automation improves the measurement.

title: Automating Antenna Pattern Testing
text:
Why I Made These Decisions


Wood for the manual mount
Why: Metal near an antenna can reflect and distort the signal being measured. Wood is RF-quiet, cheap, and fast to cut, which suited a first baseline test.


Test the FRPA before the CRPA
Why: The FRPA is a simpler antenna, so it lets us debug the chamber setup, the positioner, and our process before spending test time on the sponsor’s CRPA.


Automate the positioning
Why: Turning the table by hand and reading a printed scale is slow and adds angle error at every point. A motorized positioner hits the same angles every run and can also sweep elevation, which is impractical by hand.


Raspberry Pi + ESP32
Why: The ESP32 handles low-level motor control on the AntRunner. The Raspberry Pi runs the high-level Python test script, which is easy to edit as the test plan changes.


10° steps with a 3-second dwell
Why: This balances angular resolution against total test time. The pause lets the antenna settle after each move before a reading is taken.


Always sweep from −90° upward
Why: Returning to −90° before each new elevation row means every row is measured in the same direction, so any slack in the drive affects every row the same way.

title: Automating Antenna Pattern Testing
text:
Results So Far







Radiation pattern of the FRPA: automated AntRunner sweep (Nov 11) vs. manual hand-rotated test (Nov 4). The radial axis is relative response in dB.



Both methods show the expected shape: strongest response at boresight (0°), rolling off toward ±90°.
The manual test reads noticeably higher on the +60° to +90° side than on the matching negative angles.
The automated sweep is much more symmetric about 0°, which is closer to what we expect from this antenna.

Automating the positioner made the pattern measurement more consistent, and it is now the basis for our CRPA test plan.

title: Automating Antenna Pattern Testing
text:
Next Steps & Areas for Improvement

This project is still in progress. These are the areas I’m working on next:

Log VNA data automatically. Tie VNA data capture into the Python script, so each measurement is saved with its commanded angle and there’s no manual transcription.
Prove repeatability. Run repeated sweeps of the same antenna and report the spread at each angle (error bars), not just a single pattern.
Keep the antenna on the rotation axis. The FRPA currently sits off to one side of the positioner. A centered adapter would keep the antenna in place as it rotates, instead of swinging it around.
Clean up the RF environment. Route and secure the coax and USB cables away from the antenna, give the battery pack a proper mount, and cover nearby metal (motor, brackets) with absorber to reduce reflections.
Increase resolution where it matters. Use finer steps near boresight, and combine all elevation rows into a full 2-D pattern map.
Move to the CRPA. Apply the validated process to element-level and then array-level characterization of the CRPA.

title: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
text:
Context
How much sunlight reaches different depths in the water is a measure of water clarity and suspended pollution, both important for underwater ecosystems. Our task was to design a low-cost autonomous robot that could go to Dana Point Harbor and measure light, temperature, and depth at several depths.
Parameters we had to design around:

a target depth of about 2 m,
sensor outputs that fit the Teensy’s 0–3.3 V analog inputs,
waterproof electronics,
a robot that stays upright and holds position on the surface.

title: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
text:
My Role
This was a four-person team project. My contributions:

Sensor-interface electronics. I designed analog signal-conditioning circuits with unity-gain buffers and inverting offset op-amps. They connect an NTC thermistor, a pressure sensor, and an amorphous silicon solar cell to the Teensy microcontroller.
Firmware and data. I programmed the Teensy in the Arduino IDE for synchronized sensor logging. I then used MATLAB to calibrate the raw data and plot light and temperature against depth.
Build & assembly. I worked on building and assembling the robot and the sensor payload, including the custom winch mechanism that deploys the tethered payload.

title: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
text:
What We Built
A positively buoyant PVC surface robot carries a negatively buoyant sensor payload. A motorized winch lowers the payload in steps, so the robot can stay on the surface while it collects data vertically.





CAD of the PVC frame, with foam floats, the electronics box, and the winch.







Annotated design: frame, winch mechanism, and payload with the solar panel, thermistor, and pressure tube.







The robot on the water at Dana Point Harbor.





  
    
  

Tank test: the winch lowers the tethered sensor payload and reels it back up.

title: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
text:
How We Built It

1. Sensor circuits (sketches & schematics)
The pressure sensor only swings about 0.16 V over our 2 m depth range. I used a unity-gain buffer followed by an inverting offset amplifier (gain −11.5) to stretch that small signal across most of the ADC’s range. The thermistor uses a voltage divider with the same buffer-and-amplifier approach.





Pressure-sensor interface: unity-gain buffer, then an inverting offset amplifier (MCP602).







Thermistor voltage divider with buffer and offset amplifier (simulation).






2. Calibration

Pressure sensor: we taped its tube to a yardstick and recorded voltages at known depths, then fit a linear model (R² = 0.999).
Thermistor: we measured it in six temperature baths for a linear resistance-vs-temperature fit (R² = 0.997).
Solar cell: its open-circuit voltage is logarithmic in light, so we calibrated an exponential lux model against a lux meter.






Pressure sensor calibration: depth vs. circuit voltage.







Thermistor calibration: resistance vs. temperature.






3. Mechanical integration & payload
The electronics and the 12 V battery sit in a sealed box on the deck. The solar cell, thermistor, and pressure tube are built into a 3D-printed payload. Foam pool noodles around the frame keep the robot stable.







The 3D-printed sensor payload.




4. Deployment & data processing
The Teensy runs a stepped descent: the winch lowers the payload for 3 seconds, then pauses for 3 seconds, until it reaches maximum depth, then reels it back up. Afterwards we decoded the SD-card log in MATLAB.





Deployment location at the Dana Point fishing pier.







Logged light, temperature, and depth over the deployment.

title: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
text:
Why We Made These Decisions


Inverting offset amplifier (gain −11.5)
Why: The pressure sensor’s raw output only moved from about 0.85 V to 1.01 V over 2 m. Amplifying and offsetting it maps the surface to about 2.7 V and maximum depth to about 1.0 V, using far more of the ADC’s resolution.


Unity-gain buffers first
Why: The buffer isolates each sensor from the amplifier stage, so the gain circuit doesn’t load the sensor and distort its reading.


Solar cell wired straight to the ADC
Why: Its open-circuit voltage tops out around 3.3–3.4 V, already matching the ADC range. The Teensy’s high input impedance means the cell runs unloaded, so no extra circuitry was needed.


Stepped descent (3 s move / 3 s pause)
Why: The pauses give the sensors time to settle at each depth, and they keep readings away from electrical noise from the running motor. You can see the steps in the depth plot.


Winch motor at 3 V
Why: Lifting the payload needs about 0.29 lb·in of torque. At 3 V the motor still gives about 8.25 in·lb, a large margin, at about 30 RPM. That gives a slow, controlled 2.35 in/s descent.


Foam floats on a PVC frame
Why: The floats around the perimeter keep the center of buoyancy well above the center of mass, so the robot resists capsizing while the winch works.

title: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
text:
Results


1.84 m Max payload depth


~100k → 88k lux Light, surface to max depth


R² = 0.999 Pressure calibration


10 Hz Synchronized logging









Light intensity vs. depth with an exponential fit.



The robot deployed at Dana Point Harbor and recorded synchronized depth, light, and temperature data.
The depth trace clearly shows the programmed descent steps.
Light dropped steeply with depth, as theory predicts for a coastal harbor.
What failed: saltwater got past the thermistor’s epoxy and shorted it, so its reading jumped to the maximum (railed) about 25 seconds into the dive. The same epoxy had held up in freshwater testing at pHake Lake.

title: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle
text:
What I Learned & Would Improve

Iterating on these:

Waterproof for saltwater, not just freshwater. Use fortified epoxy around the thermistor and seal every electrical connection, then validate the sensors in saltwater before deploying.
Keep the solar cell facing up. The cell likely flipped on the way back up, producing false low readings.
Avoid saturation near the surface. The unloaded cell clips at our 100,000 lux limit in bright sun.
Tune sampling timing for more stable readings at each depth step.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard
text:
Picture of the AES-128 FPGA Accelerator Hardware setup showing indicator LED illuminated on successful ciphertext verification.
In this lab, a hardware accelerator for 128-bit Advanced Encryption Standard was designed and implemented on an iCE40 UP5K FPGA, interfacing with an STM32L432KC microcontroller over Serial Peripheral Interface. Following the specifications outlined in the NIST FIPS-197 standard, the MCU transmits a 128-bit plaintext message and a 128-bit cipher key to the FPGA over SPI while asserting a load control signal. Once the transfer completes, the load signal is deasserted and the FPGA sequentially executes the ten rounds of the AES-128 algorithm byte substitution (SubBytes), row shifting (ShiftRows), column mixing (MixColumns), round key addition (AddRoundKey), and round key generation (KeyExpansion). Upon completion, the FPGA asserts a done flag and shifts the resulting 128-bit ciphertext back to the MCU over SPI, which verifies the output against the expected FIPS-197 Appendix B test vector and illuminates a status LED.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard
text:
Design and Testing Methodology

System Architecture
Implementing all ten rounds of AES-128 combinationally would exceed the Lookup Table capacity of the iCE40 UP5K FPGA so a single round datapath is reused across ten sequential encryption rounds. To conserve logic cells, the S-Box byte substitutions (sbox_sync) are mapped to the FPGA’s Embedded Block RAMs (EBRs) rather than combinational LUTs. Sixteen sbox_sync instances are used in parallel within aes_sub_bytes to substitute all 16 bytes of the 128-bit state simultaneously, and four sbox_sync instances are used within aes_key_expansion to perform the SubWord operation, consuming 20 of the 30 available EBR blocks on the iCE40 UP5K. Each round executes across two clock cycles:

WAIT State: The current 128-bit state (XORed with the round key via aes_add_round_key) and the rotated key word are presented to the address inputs of the 20 sbox_sync BRAM blocks.On the next rising clock edge, the substituted bytes are latched at the BRAM outputs.
CALC State: At the rising clock edge, update_regs asserts to latch next_round_key into current_round_key and next_mixed_text into current_mixed_text (and on Round 10, shifted_text into round_10_shifted_text to bypass MixColumns per FIPS-197 Section 5.1).

Using this two-cycle-per-round architecture, all ten rounds complete in 21 clock cycles after load is deasserted, after which the FSM enters the RETURN state and asserts done.


MCU and FPGA SPI Interface
The provided MCU starter code configures SPI1 on pins PB3 (SCK), PB4 (MISO/SDO), and PB5 (MOSI/SDI) with clock polarity CPOL = 0 and clock phase CPHA = 0. Pin PA5 drives the LOAD signal, PA6 monitors the DONE signal from the FPGA, PA11 and PA9 / PA10 drive indicator LEDs for pass/fail verification. On the FPGA side, the internal high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) is configured with a divider of 2'b11 to supply a 6 MHz system clock (clk) to aes_corefor the combinational path through aes_row_shift and mixcolumns.


Block Diagram
 Figure 1: Top-level and submodule hardware block diagram of the AES-128 FPGA accelerator.
 Figure 1b: Block diagram of the aes_core module.
 Figure 1c: Block diagram of the aes_spi module.
The top-level lab7_ijp instantiates the 6 MHz HSOSC , the aes_spi shift-register interface, and aes_core. Inside aes_core, control logic is isolated in aes_controller, which outputs current_round, update_regs, and done. Multiplexers select key and plaintext during Round 1 (current_round == 4'd1), and select the registered current_round_key and current_mixed_text during Rounds 2 through 10. A final aes_add_round_key instance (add_key_10) XORs round_10_shifted_text with Round 10’s expanded key to produce the final cyphertext.


Finite State Machine Design
 Figure 2: State transition diagram for aes_controller.
As shown in Figure 2, aes_controller has four states:

START (2'b00): Entered synchronously whenever load is asserted. Initializes current_round to 1 and keeps done low. Transitions to WAIT once load is deasserted (load == 0).
WAIT (2'b01): Waits one clock cycle for the 20 synchronous sbox_sync EBR modules in aes_sub_bytes and aes_key_expansion to latch their substituted byte outputs. Unconditionally transitions to CALC.
CALC (2'b10): Asserts update_regs = 1'b1 to capture the newly computed round key and mixed column state (or Round 10 shifted state) on the next clock edge, and increments current_round. Transitions back to WAIT if current_round < 10, or to RETURN when current_round == 10.
RETURN (2'b11): Holds done = 1'b1 (with current_round == 11) so aes_spi can capture and shift out the final cyphertext to the MCU. Remains in RETURN until load is asserted for a new encryption request.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard
text:
AI Prototype Reflection
Output Quality & Approach:
(Prompt 1): When given the explicit FIPS-197 context, the LLM generated a highly specific, ready-to-use AES-128 KeyExpansion module. It correctly inferred the 10 rounds, hardcoded the exact Rcon values in a case statement, and implemented a clean, sequential XOR chain.
(Prompt 2): When provided only generic pseudocode, the LLM took a much more parameterized approach. It utilized generate for loops, genvar, and parameters (Nk, Nr) to unroll the logic. It also correctly inferred that the Rcon values would need to be supplied as an external array since it lacked the context of what those constants should be. The second prompt forced the LLM to use generate and genvar loops.
Synthesis: Prompt 1 correctly synthesized but Prompt 2 did not. The LLM’s output for Prompt 2 was a generic, parameterized module that would require additional context to synthesize correctly. Prompt 1’s output was a complete, synthesizable module that could be directly integrated into the larger AES datapath.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
In this lab, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was configured to measure the rotational velocity and direction of a 25GA-370 brushed DC motor. A quadrature encoder attached to the motor generates pulse signals that were tracked using hardware interrupts. By triggering external interrupts (EXTI) on both the rising and falling edges of the two out-of-phase encoder channels, the system achieves high-resolution measurements to accurately calculate and display the motor’s speed in revolutions per second (rev/s) at a 1 Hz update rate.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
Hardware Specifications & Schematic
The quadrature encoder utilizes two Hall effect sensors to measure the changing magnetic field as the motor shaft rotates. The sensors output 5V logic signals. Because the STM32L432KC operates on 3.3V logic, the encoder’s A and B channels were connected specifically to pins PA8 and PA6, which are 5V-tolerant.
 Figure 2: Schematic of the off-board encoder circuit.
On-board MCU components and internal pull-ups are not replicated in this schematic; they can be referenced in the motherboard schematic here. View the Motherboard Schematic

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
Software and Microcontroller Design
The system architecture is divided into a high-level application loop (main.c) and a encoder driver (encoder.c and encoder.h). The driver initializes the GPIO pins, routes the EXTI lines using the SYSCFG registers, and configures the Nested Vector Interrupt Controller (NVIC) to trigger the EXTI9_5_IRQHandler on every logic transition.

Flowchart
 Figure 3: Flowchart illustrating the main loop, setups, and interrupt sequence of the system.


Velocity and Direction Calculations
The 25GA-370 motor has a specified Pulse Per Revolution (PPR) of 408. Because the interrupt service routine (ISR) triggers on both the rising and falling edges of both Channel A and Channel B, there are 4 distinct state transitions per pulse. This yields a total resolution of 408 X 4 = 1,632 counts per full motor revolution.
The ISR updates a shared volatile int32_t counter. Every 1000 milliseconds (managed by TIM2), the main loop briefly disables the EXTI interrupts to atomically read and reset this counter.
Velocity is calculated using the following equation:
\(\text{Velocity (rev/s)} = \frac{\text{Current Count}}{408 \text{ pulses/rev} \times 4 \text{ edges/pulse}}\)
Direction is determined in the ISR by comparing the previous state of the two pins to their current state. For example, if both pins were LOW (00) and Channel A transitions HIGH (10), Channel A is leading, indicating clockwise (CW) rotation. The calculated speed is then paired with this direction state for output over the ITM debug channel.


Interrupts vs. Polling
While a continuous polling loop can detect logic changes, it introduces reliability issues at high speeds.
At a 12V supply, the motor spins at roughly 150 RPM, or 2.5 rev/s. Given our resolution of 1,632 edges per revolution, the encoder generates a signal state change at a frequency of: \(2.5 \text{ rev/s} \times 1,632 \text{ edges/rev} = 4,080 \text{ Hz}\)
This means an edge occurs approximately every 245 μs. According to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, a polling loop would need to successfully sample the pins at greater than 8,160 Hz (a loop time of 122 μs) to avoid missing a pulse. However, our main loop utilizes a blocking 1,000 ms delay and relies on floating-point printf operations. During this time, the polling loop is entirely paused, meaning thousands of encoder pulses would be missed, resulting in aliasing and an inaccurate velocity calculation.
By utilizing EXTI interrupts, the MCU bypasses the main loop entirely. The ISR takes only a few dozen clock cycles to execute (less than 1 μs on an 80 MHz clock). Therefore, the interrupt based code guarantees zero missed pulses at maximum motor speeds, while still registering non-zero velocities at low speeds where a 1 Hz polling loop might incorrectly register stationary behavior due to clipping.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
Results and Requirements Statement
The design meets all requirements outlined in the Lab 5 specifications: * The system utilizes interrupts to read both edges of both encoder channels, capturing all pulses at normal and high speeds. * Motor velocity is calculated in rev/s and displayed via the ITM debug channel at an update rate of 1 Hz. * The measured speed appropriately registers as 0.000 rev/s when the motor is stationary. According to the datasheet, at 12V the motor spins at roughly 150 RPM (2.5 rev/s). My debug terminal measured ~2.9 rev/s at 12V, verifying that the calculations and direction states match the true physical motor speed.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts
text:
AI Prototype

LLM Prompt

Write me interrupt handlers to interface with a quadrature encoder. I’m using the STM32L432KC, what pins should I connect the encoder to in order to allow it to easily trigger the interrupts?



Reflection
Quality of Output The quality of ChatGPT 5.0’s response was good but had some downsides. The LLM accurately explained quadrature decoding and provided a bit-shifting state machine to handle the logic. However, it recommended pins PA0 and PA1. According to the STM32L432KC datasheet, these pins are not 5V-tolerant so connecting our 5V lab encoder directly to them could damage the board. The LLM also generated code using the STM32 Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) library instead of using CMSIS.
Code Generation Comparison Because of the HAL library usage, the generated code would not compile in my Segger Embedded Studio setup. My final design manually configures the SYSCFG, EXTI, and NVIC registers and relies on the EXTI9_5_IRQHandler mapped to the 5V-tolerant PA6 and PA8 pins. For the decoding logic, the LLM used a switch statement evaluating a 4-bit previous/current state ((encoder_state << 2) | new_state). I used explicit if/else logic gates in my implementation to make the hardware-level state transitions more readable and easier to debug.

title: Lab 3: Keypad Scanner
text:
This lab focuses on designing a circuit interface to read a 4x4 matrix keypad and display the results on a dual seven-segment display. The design must display the last two hexadecimal digits pressed, with the most recent entry appearing on the right. Because mechanical switches are prone to bouncing making and breaking connections rapidly over a few milliseconds, the system must implement a debouncing strategy to ensure each key press is registered exactly once. Furthermore, the system must handle multi-press edge cases, ignoring additional inputs if a button is already held down and refusing to lock up if multiple buttons are pressed simultaneously. The design was written in SystemVerilog, verified using Questa Sim, and synthesized for the UPduino v3.1 FPGA.

Methods

Fully Synchronous Architecture & Clocking
To manage both the fast 24MHz system clock and the slower human scale input requirements, a fully synchronous architecture was installed using clock enables. A 17-bit counter module divides the 24MHz clock to generate a single-cycle tick approximately every 183Hz. This tick signal acts as an enable for the finite state machine and the multiplexer toggle, ensuring all sequential logic is evaluated safely on the primary 24MHz clock edge.


Debouncing Strategy & Tradeoffs
Switch bouncing was handled through the FSM’s state transition timing. Because the FSM only evaluates state changes when the tick is high. When a press is detected, the FSM must traverse from a scan state (rX), to a press detect state (pX), to a sync state (sX), and finally to an enable state (eX). Therefore, by making tick an arbitrary value through experimentation, this creates a delay between initial contact and input registration, outlasting typical mechanical switch bounce.

Tradeoffs: This FSM-based sampling method is highly resource-efficient and inherently synchronous. It eliminates the need for internal counter registers inside the FSM module. The primary tradeoff is a slight latency between the physical press and visual output. An alternative method running the FSM at 24MHz and using a large internal counter (counting to 500,000) would provide finer control over the exact debounce delay, but clutters the FSM logic with timers. Relying on a system-wide tick keeps the FSM strictly focused on state routing.



Multi-Press and Metastability Handling
To resolve metastability when reading asynchronous human inputs, a 2-flop synchronizer module aligns the column inputs to the 24MHz clock before they reach the FSM. To prevent the system from locking up or misfiring when multiple buttons are pressed, the FSM utilizes decoder logic (press = 1 ONLY if exactly one column is active). If multiple buttons are mashed, the FSM ignores the input and continues scanning. Once a valid press is registered, the FSM locks the active column into a first_col register and enters a wait state (wX). It remains trapped in this wait state as long as the original button is held, preventing auto-repeating digits. If multiple buttons are held down and all but one are released, the FSM will cycle back to the scan states, recognize the newly isolated button, and register it properly as a new single key press.

section: AI Prototype Reflection: Monolithic vs. Modular Prompting
text:
AI Prototype Reflection: Monolithic vs. Modular Prompting
The purpose of this AI prototype was to explore how Large Language Models handle design modularity when generating SystemVerilog for digital logic, specifically comparing a monolithic, all-at-once prompt against decomposed prompts.

Monolithic vs. Modular Prompt Performance
When given the monolithic prompt (Prototype A), ChatGPT5 successfully decomposed the design into four distinct modules without explicit instruction. A clock divider, a keypad scanner, a seven-segment multiplexer, and a top-level integration module. However, its initial implementation of the finite state machine inside the keypad scanner was faulty. It used a single enumerated state variable (S_SCAN0 through S_SCAN3 and S_HELD) to handle both the column iteration and the debounce wait state.
By contrast, decomposing the prompts (Prototype B) forced the LLM to separate the physical row and column scanning from the debouncing logic. This modular approach produced a much cleaner architecture where the scanner simply outputted a continuous stream of pressed keys, and a dedicated key_registration module filtered those into a single new_key pulse. Modularizing the prompts significantly improved the readability of the FSMs by enforcing strict separation.
During synthesis in Lattice Radiant, I encountered two specific errors. The first was an unknown module SB_HFOSC error. When I fed this back to the LLM, it correctly identified that SB_HFOSC is a Lattice-specific primitive that might fail and it advised me to remove the direct instantiation and pass the clock in as a top-level port instead. The second issue was a VERI-1063 error stating that keypad_scanner was an unknown module inside clock_enable.sv. The LLM identified this issue as a file structure issue, pointing out that I had likely pasted all the generated modules into a single file named clock_enable.sv, meaning the synthesis tool couldn’t find the keypad_scanner definition when compiling other files. Once I separated the code into proper .sv files as the LLM suggested, the design synthesized successfully.
In future workflows, I will use the decomposed prompting strategy from the start. Asking an LLM to generate an entire system at once often results in merged logic and tightly coupled FSMs. Breaking the design down into specific modules yields hardware that is much easier to read, test, and debug.

Documentation
The project was constructed using three system verilog modules including a top-level module (e155_lab1_ivan.sv), a sequential counter (e155_lab1_counter_ivan.sv), and a combinational decoder (seven_segment.sv). Figure 2 below shows the block diagram of the modules.
 Figure 2: Block diagram.

LED Implementation & Clock Divider
By inspection of the truth tables, led[0] is driven by the XOR of inputs s[0] and s[1], while led[1] is driven by the AND of inputs s[2] and s[3]. These were implemented using assign statements in the top module.
To generate a blinking frequency of 2.4 Hz for led[2], a sequential counter module was designed. The 48 MHz on-board HSOSC was first divided in half using the CLKHF_DIV(2'b01) parameter, producing a 24 MHz clock. A blink rate of 2.4 Hz requires the LED to complete a full ON-OFF cycle 2.4 times per second, meaning the signal must toggle its state 4.8 times per second. By dividing 24,000,000 Hz by 4.8, we must toggle 5,000,000 clock cycles. A zero-indexed counter was implemented to trigger a toggle and reset upon reaching a max count of 4999999.


7-Segment Display Implementation
The 7-segment display was designed using combinational logic to map the sixteen DIP switch states to output 0 to F. Figure 3 shows the schematic for how the display, LEDs, and pull-up resistors on the DIP switches were wired.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text:
Methods

Time-Multiplexing Setup
Time-multiplexing allows a common hardware resource to be shared for several purposes at different times. A single seven-segment decoder was used to drive both digits of the display. To control which digit was active, the common anode of each display was toggled sequentially. Because the anode requires more current than the FPGA can directly supply, 2N3906 PNP transistors were utilized to switch the current.
 Figure 1: Complete Dual Seven Segment Display and Keypad Breadboard.


Matrix Keypad Scanning
The matrix keypad contains four rows and four columns, connected to 8 total pins. The scanning module asserts signals on each row one at a time and observes the values of the columns. To prevent short circuits when multiple keys in the same column are pressed simultaneously, an open-drain conversion circuit was built using 2N3904 NPN transistors. The FPGA drives the base of the transistor, the emitter is grounded, and the collector connects to the keypad row, allowing the output to float when deasserted. Internal pull-up resistors were configured on the FPGA column input pins to read the logic levels correctly.


FPGA Project
The top-level design connects the inputs and outputs to achieve the multiplexing and scanning. Table 1 outlines the primary signals used in the project.

Documentation
The design includes a single time-multiplexed seven-segment decoder module, a counter module, a scanning module, and a top-level module. The top-level design only includes instances of these submodules and assign statements to route the multiplexing and scanning logic. Figure 1 below shows the block diagram of the system.
 Figure 1: Block diagram representing the logic structure.

Counter & State Machines
All counting logic was handled by a single module. This module was instantiated twice in the top level. The first instance (mux_cntr) was parameterized to 17 bits to divide the 24 MHz clock down to a smaller frequency, ensuring the switching is imperceptible to the human eye.
The scanning module utilizes a 25-bit counter. The top two bits were extracted to create a 4-state machine that rotates the output sequence across the keypad rows (1000, 0100, 0010, 0001).


Schematic & Electrical Calculations
Figure 2 shows the complete schematic detailing the off-board components, including the 4x4 keypad, the dual 7-segment display, the LEDs, and the transistor driver circuits.
 Figure 2: Schematic of off-board components and transistor circuits.
Calculations were performed to ensure current draw and sink on all FPGA pins remained below the recommended limits. According to the iCE40 UltraPlus data sheet, the maximum output low current and output high current for the LVCMOS 3.3V standard is 8 mA.
Figure 3 provides the calculations for the series base resistors used on the NPN and PNP transistors. Accounting for a 3.3V logic high and a typical 0.7V base-emitter forward voltage, resistors were selected to limit the FPGA pin current well below the 8 mA threshold.

AI Reflection
AI Prompt 1 (Without Context): Write SystemVerilog HDL to time multiplex a single seven segment decoder (that decodes from four bits to a common anode seven segment display) to decode two sets of input bits and drive two sets of seven output bits.
AI Prompt 2 (With Lab 1 Context Attached): Write SystemVerilog HDL to time multiplex a single seven segment decoder (that decodes from four bits to a common anode seven segment display) to decode two sets of input bits and drive two sets of seven output bits. Use the seven segment decoder and oscillator provided in the attached files.
Reflection on the AI Prototype:
When given the first prompt with no context, ChatGPT-5 generated a generic multiplexer. It created its own seven-segment case statement from scratch and used an arbitrary clk input. It also implemented a sequential flip-flop block to alternate registering the outputs to two completely separate 7-bit buses (seg0 and seg1).
Adding the Lab 1 files as context in the second prompt improved the hardware accuracy of the response. ChatGPT correctly instantiated the Lattice HSOSC to generate the clock, reused my exact seven_segment combinational module from Lab 1, and implemented a proper counter to divide the 24 MHz clock down to a 1 kHz switching frequency.
However, the generated code still contained flaws based on my prompt’s phrasing. Because I asked it to drive two sets of seven output bits, the LLM created two 7-bit outputs (seg0 and seg1). In reality, time-multiplexing a dual display involves sharing a single 7-bit segment bus and using transistors to toggle the common anodes one at a time.
I would rate the quality of the output an 8/10. The SystemVerilog syntax was great and it correctly utilized always_comb and always_ff blocks. The code would synthesize in Lattice Radiant the first time around without syntax errors.

Hardware Design
Driving an 8-ohm speaker directly from the microcontroller’s GPIO pins would draw excessive current, risking permanent damage to the MCU. To safely buffer the signal and provide sufficient driving current, an LM386 audio amplifier was placed between the MCU and the speaker.
The audio signal is generated via PWM on pin PB6, which corresponds to the complementary timer output TIM16_CH1N. This signal is routed through a 10 kΩ potentiometer acting as a voltage divider, allowing the attenuation of the input signal to the LM386 amplifier for volume control. The output of the LM386 passes through a 220 µF series capacitor accompanied by a 0.05 µF capacitor and 10 Ω resistor in series to ground to provide high-frequency stability. Additionally, pin PB3 is configured as a standard digital output connected internally to the Nucleo board’s LD3 LED, flashing in sync with every played note to provide visual feedback.
 Figure 2: Schematic of the off-board audio amplification circuit.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Software Architecture
The software manipulates memory-mapped registers directly using custom C structs (FLASH_TypeDef, GPIO, TIM_TypeDef, RCC_TypeDef) to enable clocks, configure pins, and control timers. Two hardware timers coordinate the audio playback:

TIM16 (Pitch Generation): TIM16 is configured in PWM Mode 1 to generate the square waves for the audio frequencies. The system clock (80 MHz) is stepped down using a prescaler (PSC) of 79, resulting in a 1 MHz timer clock. The Auto-Reload Register (ARR) is updated for each note to set the pitch, while the Capture Compare Register (CCR1) is set to half the ARR value to maintain a 50% duty cycle. Because PB6 is a complementary output, bit 2 (CC1NE) of the CCER register is toggled to enable and disable the audio output, properly handling rests (0 Hz).
TIM15 (Duration Control): TIM15 manages the timing delays that dictate how long each note is held. It utilizes a prescaler of 3000 to slow the timer count, preventing 16-bit register overflow during long notes. The program stops execution by using the TIM15 Status Register (SR) update interrupt flag (UIF) until the specified duration elapses.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
System Calculations

Frequency Range and Duration Range
TIM16 generates the PWM frequency, fed by an 80 MHz clock with a prescaler (PSC) of 79. TIM15 manages the note delays using a prescaler of 3000.
 Figure 3: Calculations of the Frequency Range and Duration Range .


Frequency Accuracy
The design must replicate notes within a 1% accuracy margin between 220 Hz and 1000 Hz. The error stems from integer truncation when calculating the ARR value. Checking these bounds is sufficient to prove compliance. Because integer truncation causes the frequency error, higher frequencies which require smaller ARR values suffer from larger percentage errors.
 Figure 4: Calculations of the Frequency Accuracy across 220Hz to 1,000Hz .

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Statement of Requirements
The digital audio system meets all Proficiency and Excellence requirements for Lab 4. The design successfully plays both Für Elise and the Super Mario Bros. theme at their correct tempos. The hardware utilizes an LM386 audio amplifier to safely drive the speaker and includes a potentiometer for volume control. The software defines all memory-mapped registers manually using custom C structs, avoiding CMSIS headers entirely. Note durations and rests are managed using hardware timers, and all frequency calculations avoid division-by-zero errors.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio

Quality and Speed of Output: The quality of the ChatGPT5’s output was faster than manually searching through the 1600-page STM32L432KC Reference Manual. Instead of utilizing Ctrl-F to hunt for scattered information across the RCC and Timer chapters, the LLM immediately synthesized the necessary configuration steps and provided the core equation for frequency.
Reasoning and Timer Selection: The LLM recommended using TIM2 because of its 32-bit counter and 4-channel GPIO routing. Because the target frequency range was only 220 Hz to 1 kHz, the 16-bit counters of TIM15 and TIM16 were more than sufficient, and TIM16_CH1N routed perfectly to my chosen output pin (PB6).
Document Search The most impressive part of the interaction occurred when the RM0394 manual was attached to the prompt. As a document search assistant, the LLM proved better to standard keyword searches.

In Lab 6, an Internet of Things (IoT) device was designed and implemented using the STM32L432KC microcontroller, an ESP8266 WiFi module, and a DS1722 digital temperature sensor. The goal of this lab was to develop an embedded system capable of reading environmental data over a Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) and serving it to a web interface over a USART connection. Users can interact with the webpage to toggle a hardware LED, select the temperature sensor’s resolution (8 to 12 bits), and view real-time temperature updates.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
System Architecture and Hardware Design
The hardware for this lab consists of three main components: 1. STM32L432KC MCU: Acts as the central processor, managing the SPI and USART peripherals. 2. ESP8266 WiFi Module: Configured as an access point and web server. It communicates with the MCU via a 125000 baud USART link (with RX and TX lines crossed). 3. DS1722 Digital Thermometer: Interfaced with the MCU over SPI. The sensor requires an active-high Chip Enable (CE) and operates in continuous conversion mode.

Schematic
 Figure 2: Schematic of the IoT Device.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Software and Microcontroller Design

SPI Driver Implementation
A custom SPI driver was written using the CMSIS device templates to interface with the DS1722. - Pins: PA5 (SCK), PB4 (MISO), PB5 (MOSI), and PA8 (CE). - Configuration: The SPI peripheral (SPI1) was configured for a 625 kHz clock (derived from the 80 MHz system clock). The DS1722 requires a clock phase (CPHA) of 1 and a clock polarity (CPOL) of 0. - Data Handling: The 8-bit FIFO reception threshold (FRXTH) was enabled to allow proper byte-by-byte transmission and reception using the SPI1->DR register. Software Slave Management (SSM) was utilized so the active-high CE pin could be controlled manually as a standard GPIO output.


Temperature Conversion
The DS1722 outputs temperature as a 16-bit two’s complement value. The MCU reads the LSB (0x01) and MSB (0x02) registers, concatenates them into a signed 16-bit integer, and divides by 256.0 to calculate the temperature in Celsius. This automatically handles both positive and negative temperatures across the sensor’s full range.


USART and Webserver Logic
The ESP8266 forwards HTTP requests to the MCU in the format /REQ:<command>\n. The MCU parses this string to: - Update the LED state (e.g., ledon, ledoff). - Update the DS1722 resolution (e.g., res8 through res12) by writing to its configuration register (0x80). After processing the request, the MCU generates an HTML string containing the current temperature, resolution, and LED status, and transmits it back to the ESP8266. State-tracking variables ensure the LED and resolution do not reset unexpectedly when the page is refreshed.

text:

Web Interface
The web interface successfully loads and displays the current temperature. Toggling the LED and changing the resolution updates the hardware and the webpage accurately.

To verify the SPI protocol, an oscilloscope was used to capture a full SPI read transaction. The trace demonstrates the active-high CE, the clock idling low, and data being sampled on the correct clock edges (CPHA=1).

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
AI Prototype Reflection
When comparing the LLM’s proficiency between frontend web development and low-level embedded C, it is clear that the AI is better at frontend web development. For the HTML prompt, the LLM instantly generated a highly polished, responsive dashboard complete with CSS styling, interactive toggle switches, and even a simulated Chart.js graph. Because web development relies on universal standards and flexible environments, the AI’s frontend output was structurally complete and visually impressive out of the box. Conversely, while the LLM correctly identified the DS1722’s unique datasheet requirements—such as an active-high Chip Enable, CPHA = 1, and the \(1/256^\circ\text{C}\) two’s complement conversion its embedded C code was difficult to integrate. It rigidly hardcoded assumptions about the hardware (assigning SPI to PA4-PA7 instead of the project’s specific wiring) and used raw bit-shifting macros that didn’t perfectly align with the STM32L432KC CMSIS templates.
Ultimately, the LLM served as a good conceptual guide, but a poor direct code generator for hardware specific tasks. Its detailed breakdown of the SPI initialization requirements and the scaling mathematics were incredibly helpful for verifying the driver’s logic. However, the experience reinforced that while AI can practically write a web app for you, embedded systems require too much board-specific context such as shared pins, specific header macros, and register-level specifics to blindly trust AI-generated C code.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Conclusion
The design meets all the requirements for Proficiency and Excellence. The IoT device successfully hosts a web server, controls hardware peripherals, and correctly parses two’s complement SPI data across multiple resolutions.

text:
In E155: Microprocessor Systems, I designed and built digital electronic systems using FPGAs, microcontrollers, and other hardware components to perform specific tasks. Through hands-on labs and continuous iteration, I developed skills in embedded programming, FPGA development, and systematic debugging.
FPGA SystemVerilog STM32 / C SPI Interrupts Questa Sim







Lab 1

FPGA & MCU Setup & Testing
The purpose of this lab was to assemble a development board with an FPGA and MCU on-board. Then, digital designs were implemented using SystemVerilog to verify the hardware functionality. The board utilizes the onboard high-speed oscillator to drive a 2.4 Hz LED blink, map discrete logic to additional LEDs based on DIP switch inputs, and decode a 4-bit binary input to display hexadecimal characters 0 through F on a 7-segment display.
Learn More About Lab 1








Lab 2

Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
The purpose of this lab was to implement a time-multiplexing scheme to efficiently use the FPGA’s I/O pins. The design drives two independent hexadecimal numbers on a dual seven-segment display using only a single seven-segment decoder module. Additionally, a scanning circuit was developed to interact with a 4x4 matrix keypad by driving its rows and reading its columns. The system was designed using SystemVerilog and verified using Questa Sim before physical implementation on the UPduino v3.1 development board.
Learn More About Lab 2








Lab 3

Keypad Scanner
This lab focuses on designing a circuit interface to read a 4x4 matrix keypad and display the results on a dual seven-segment display. The design must display the last two hexadecimal digits pressed, with the most recent entry appearing on the right. Because mechanical switches are prone to bouncing making and breaking connections rapidly over a few milliseconds, the system must implement a debouncing strategy to ensure each key press is registered exactly once. Furthermore, the system must handle multi-press edge cases, ignoring additional inputs if a button is already held down and refusing to lock up if multiple buttons are pressed simultaneously. The design was written in SystemVerilog, verified using Questa Sim, and synthesized for the UPduino v3.1 FPGA.
Learn More About Lab 3








Lab 4

Digital Audio
This lab focuses on utilizing the internal peripheral timers of the STM32L432KC microcontroller to generate digital audio. By producing precisely timed PWM square waves, the microcontroller functions as a digital synthesizer capable of playing musical sequences with varying pitches and durations. The system was programmed in C to play Beethoven’s Für Elise and the Super Mario Bros. theme by interacting directly with memory-mapped hardware registers. An external LM386 audio amplifier circuit was constructed to safely drive an 8-ohm speaker, incorporating a potentiometer for manual volume control.
Learn More About Lab 4








Lab 5

Interrupts
In this lab, the STM32L432KC microcontroller was configured to measure the rotational velocity and direction of a 25GA-370 brushed DC motor. A quadrature encoder attached to the motor generates pulse signals that were tracked using hardware interrupts. By triggering external interrupts (EXTI) on both the rising and falling edges of the two out-of-phase encoder channels, the system achieves high-resolution measurements to accurately calculate and display the motor’s speed in revolutions per second (rev/s) at a 1 Hz update rate.
Learn More About Lab 5








Lab 6

The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
An Internet of Things device built with the STM32L432KC microcontroller, an ESP8266 WiFi module, and a DS1722 digital temperature sensor. The MCU reads temperature data over SPI and serves it to a web interface over USART, where users can toggle an LED, select the sensor’s resolution (8 to 12 bits), and view real-time temperature updates.
Learn More About Lab 6








Lab 7

The Advanced Encryption Standard
A hardware accelerator for 128-bit AES implemented on an iCE40 UP5K FPGA following the NIST FIPS-197 standard. The STM32L432KC sends the plaintext and key over SPI, the FPGA runs ten rounds on a reused single-round datapath with S-boxes mapped to block RAM, and the ciphertext is shifted back to the MCU and verified against the FIPS-197 test vector.

title: Brachistochrone Curve Model
text:
Why We Made These Decisions


Equation Driven Curves instead of sketched splines
Why: The whole demonstration depends on each curve’s exact shape. Driving the geometry from the equations keeps the cycloid mathematically accurate, where a hand-fit spline could change the descent times.


A cheap printed prototype first
Why: Printing a small PLA version tested the curve math quickly before we spent time and material on a large build.


Twin “floating ball” rails instead of a walled ramp
Why: The ball touches only two thin edges, which cuts friction. Students can also see more of the ball from across a large classroom.


MDF, CNC-routed
Why: MDF is wear resistant, so it suits a model used for years. The CNC router reproduces the CAD curves accurately at a size too large for our laser cutter.


Hinged gate with a lip
Why: A fair race needs every ball to start at the same instant. The extra lip makes up for the steep start of the polynomial curve.


Bigger instead of smaller
Why: The client cared most about visibility. A larger model made the finishing order obvious to the naked eye, without slowing down the video.

How We Built It: Three Prototypes
We iterated through three prototypes, each one answering a question from the last.





Prototype 1: 3D-printed PLA. Curves first drawn in Desmos, then modeled in SolidWorks and printed to check the equations.







Prototype 2: laser-cut plywood. Twin-rail “floating ball” tracks and the first hinged PVC release gate.

Prove the math (Prototype 1). We plotted the curves in Desmos, modeled them in SolidWorks, and 3D printed a small PLA version. It behaved close to the predictions, which confirmed the curve equations. The next priorities were a smoother, lower-friction surface and a simultaneous release.
Improve friction and visibility (Prototype 2). We laser cut each curve twice from ¼-inch plywood and glued the two cuts about 1 inch apart, so the ball rides between two thin rails instead of in a walled channel. A half PVC pipe on two hinges released all the balls together.
Scale up (final). The client told us visibility mattered more than the original size limit, so we went bigger. I got CNC router certified, and we routed ¾-inch MDF planks down to ¼ inch, cutting two of each curve plus the base and back wall.
Finish and assemble. We sanded every edge smooth on the belt and hand sanders. Then we laid out the tracks 3 inches apart with a 1-inch gap for the ball, and fixed them with wood and hot glue.
Build the release gate. We cut a 2-inch PVC pipe in half and to 12 inches on the bandsaw, spray painted it pink, and hinged it to the back wall. A small lip lets the steep polynomial curve start at the same moment as the others.
